title: Strict diagrams as modules on a small site
statement: Let $J$ be a small category and $\mathcal C$ a small site with a sheaf $\mathcal O$ of commutative rings. On the small category $\mathcal D=J^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C$, take the Grothendieck topology generated by the families $\{(\mathrm{id}_j,V_i\to U):(j,V_i)\to(j,U)\}_i$ for coverings $\{V_i\to U\}_i$ of $\mathcal C$ (a sieve is a collection of arrows with fixed target closed under precomposition; a Grothendieck topology assigns covering sieves satisfying maximality, pullback stability and local character; a sheaf is a contravariant set-valued functor for which every matching family on a covering sieve has a unique amalgamation). The presheaf $\mathcal O_{\mathcal D}(j,U)=\mathcal O(U)$, with identity action in the $J$ direction, is a sheaf of rings. There are equivalences $\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal D)\simeq\operatorname{Fun}(J,\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C))$ and $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal O_{\mathcal D})\simeq\operatorname{Fun}(J,\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal O))$ [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category], sending a sheaf $F$ to the diagram $j\mapsto(U\mapsto F(j,U))$ and sending morphisms to their components; the module equivalence is additive and exact. For each $j\in J$, evaluation is the inverse-image functor of a morphism of topoi $e_j:\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C)\to\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal D)$ (an adjoint pair $e_j^{-1}\dashv e_{j*}$ with $e_j^{-1}$ preserving finite limits). Its right adjoint, in the diagram description, is $(e_{j*}A)(k)=\prod_{\alpha:k\to j}A$, with structure maps induced by precomposition. We have $e_j^{-1}\mathcal O_{\mathcal D}=\mathcal O$, and the induced inverse image on module sheaves (inverse image followed by extension of scalars along this ring identification) is exact evaluation.

proof.text: For a sieve $R$ on $(j,U)$ put $R_j=\{f:V\to U\mid(\mathrm{id}_j,f)\in R\}$. Declare $R$ covering when $R_j$ covers $U$. This satisfies maximality. For an arrow $(\alpha,f):(k,V)\to(j,U)$, where $\alpha:j\to k$ in $J$, the vertical slice of its pullback contains $f^*R_j$: if $fh\in R_j$, then $(\alpha,fh)$ belongs to $R$ by precomposition. Thus pullback stability follows from that in $\mathcal C$. Covering sieves are upward closed directly from local character: if $S\subset T$ and $S$ covers, the pullbacks of $T$ along arrows of $S$ are maximal.

proof.text: For local character, suppose $R_j$ covers and a sieve $T$ pulls back to a covering sieve along every arrow in $R$. In particular, for every $f\in R_j$ the vertical slice of $(\mathrm{id}_j,f)^*T$ is $f^*T_j$, which covers. Local character in $\mathcal C$ gives that $T_j$ covers. Hence the rule is a topology. The sieve generated by a vertical covering family has vertical slice the sieve generated by that family in $\mathcal C$, so is covering. Conversely, every covering $R$ contains such a vertical covering family (take all arrows of its covering slice, or an original covering family contained in that slice). Any topology containing these families contains $R$ by upward closure. This identifies the rule with the generated topology of the statement.

proof.text: A presheaf $P$ on $\mathcal D$ is precisely the following data: presheaves $P_j$ on $\mathcal C$ and natural maps $P(\alpha):P_j\to P_k$ for $\alpha:j\to k$, respecting identities and composition. Indeed every restriction along $(\alpha,f):(k,V)\to(j,U)$ factors as $P_j(U)\xrightarrow{P(\alpha)_U}P_k(U)\to P_k(V)$. The two coordinate restrictions commute by functoriality in the product category; conversely this displayed formula defines a presheaf from the stated data. The same factorization identifies natural transformations with their component natural transformations.

proof.text: If $P$ is a sheaf on $\mathcal D$, then $P_j$ is a sheaf on $\mathcal C$. Given a matching family $t_f\in P_j(V)$ on a covering sieve $S$ of $U$, extend it to the sieve generated by its vertical arrows by the formula $t_{(\alpha,f)}=P(\alpha)_V(t_f)$. An arrow is in this generated sieve exactly when its $\mathcal C$ coordinate lies in $S$. The formula respects precomposition by the naturality in step 3 and the matching identities for $t$. Unique gluing on $\mathcal D$ therefore gives unique gluing of the original family in $P_j(U)$.

proof.text: Conversely suppose every $P_j$ is a sheaf. For a matching family $t$ on a covering sieve $R$ of $(j,U)$, glue its vertical part on $R_j$ to $s\in P_j(U)$. For $(\alpha,f):(k,V)\to(j,U)$ in $R$, the sections $P(\alpha,f)s$ and $t_{(\alpha,f)}$ agree after every $h:W\to V$ with $fh\in R_j$, by matching compatibility with the vertical arrow $(\mathrm{id}_j,fh)$ and its precomposition by $(\alpha,\mathrm{id}_W)$. The sieve $f^*R_j$ covers $V$, so separatedness of $P_k$ makes those sections equal. Uniqueness follows by restricting any amalgamation to $R_j$. Thus $P$ is a sheaf.

proof.text: Steps 3--5 restrict the inverse constructions on presheaves and transformations to sheaves. Their composites return the same values and restriction maps, giving the stated sheaf equivalence. The constant diagram on the ring sheaf $\mathcal O$ assembles to $\mathcal O_{\mathcal D}$; step 5 proves its underlying presheaf is a sheaf, and its ring operations are the given ones on $\mathcal O(U)$, commuting with all restrictions. Hence it is a sheaf of commutative rings.

proof.text: Use the definition of module sheaves in [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. At $(j,U)$ an $\mathcal O_{\mathcal D}$-module is an $\mathcal O(U)$-module. Restriction in the $J$ direction is $\mathcal O(U)$-linear because the ring restriction is identity, while restriction in the $\mathcal C$ direction has exactly the semilinearity required for an $\mathcal O$-module sheaf. Steps 3--5 therefore identify these data with diagrams of $\mathcal O$-modules, in both directions. Transformations are linear precisely when each component is linear, and componentwise addition is unchanged. This proves the module equivalence and its additivity.

proof.text: The category $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal O)$ is abelian by [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. For a morphism $u:M\to N$ of diagrams, form $K_j=\ker u_j$ and $Q_j=\operatorname{coker}u_j$. For $\alpha:j\to k$, the commuting square of $u$ induces $K_j\to K_k$ by the kernel universal property and $Q_j\to Q_k$ by the cokernel universal property; uniqueness proves identity and composition laws. The same universal properties assemble any componentwise factorization into a unique diagram morphism. Hence these are the kernel and cokernel in the diagram category. Image and coimage are consequently componentwise and their comparison is an isomorphism at every component, with natural inverse. The diagram category is abelian and evaluation preserves kernels and cokernels, hence is exact.

proof.text: The additive equivalence of step 7 preserves the kernel and cokernel universal properties: testing maps in the target is the same as testing their inverse images in the source, since both constructions are inverse on objects and morphisms. It therefore preserves kernels, cokernels, images and coimages, and short exact sequences. The source module category is abelian by [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category] applied to the small site $\mathcal D$. Together with step 8 this proves exactness of the equivalence and of module evaluation on $\mathcal D$.

proof.text: Products of sheaves of sets on $\mathcal C$ can be formed sectionwise: a matching family in $\prod_i A_i$ is a matching family in each $A_i$, and unique gluing in each coordinate is unique gluing in the product. The terminal singleton presheaf is a sheaf; equalizers of sheaf maps are sheaves because gluing in the source stays in the equalizer by uniqueness in the target. These sectionwise constructions satisfy their universal properties by the universal properties of products and equalizers of sets. Applying them componentwise to diagrams, with structure maps induced coordinatewise, proves their universal properties for diagrams too. Thus evaluation preserves terminal objects, products and equalizers, and hence finite limits (a finite diagram limit is the equalizer of the two maps between products indexed by its objects and arrows).

proof.text: Fix $j\in J$. For a sheaf $A$ define $(R_jA)(k)=\prod_{\alpha:k\to j}A$ using step 10. For $\beta:k\to l$, send a tuple $x$ to the tuple with $\gamma:l\to j$ coordinate $x_{\gamma\circ\beta}$. Associativity and identities in $J$ give the diagram laws. A sheaf map $A\to B$ acts on every coordinate, making $R_j$ a functor. Smallness of $J$ makes every indexing family a set, so all these products exist.

proof.text: For a diagram $F$ and a map $h:F(j)\to A$, define a transformation $F\to R_jA$ whose $\alpha:k\to j$ coordinate is $h\circ F(\alpha)$. Its naturality for $\beta:k\to l$ is the equality $hF(\gamma\beta)=hF(\gamma)F(\beta)$. Conversely, take the $\mathrm{id}_j$ coordinate of a transformation at $j$. These constructions are inverse: naturality along $\alpha:k\to j$ identifies the $\alpha$ coordinate with the $\mathrm{id}_j$ coordinate composed with $F(\alpha)$. Both constructions commute with maps in $F$ and $A$. This is the natural adjunction $\operatorname{ev}_j\dashv R_j$.

proof.text: Transfer this adjunction across the sheaf equivalence of step 6. Step 10 proves finite-limit preservation, so by the stated definition of a morphism of topoi it defines $e_j:\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C)\to\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal D)$ with inverse image evaluation and direct image $R_j$. The coefficient diagram is constant, so its evaluation is precisely $\mathcal O$, including multiplication and unit. On modules, inverse image has the componentwise action of step 7 and extension of scalars is along the identity of $\mathcal O$; the isomorphism $\mathcal O\otimes_{\mathcal O}M\to M$ is $a\otimes x\mapsto ax$, inverse $x\mapsto1\otimes x$. Thus the induced module pullback is evaluation, exact by steps 8--9.
